alalal-e82539-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 15: whether one can know with most certain knowledge whether one is worthy of eternal life.

alalal-e82539-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's (Augustine's) statement that faith is not seen in the heart as other things are, but is held by its possessor with most certain knowledge.

alalal-e82539-d1e129.summary: Objection: whoever has one virtue has all, so if I see my faith with certainty I would know I am worthy of eternal life, contrary to Ecclesiastes 9:1, Paul's 'I am not conscious of anything, but I am not thereby justified', Proverbs on the way that seems right but leads to death, and Gregory's gloss that saints weep because they do not know whether they please God.

alalal-e82539-d1e176.summary: Rejects one reply, that one sees faith but does not know whether it is gratuitously given or sanctifying: the same objection applies to sanctifying grace, which is in the soul by essence and would be seen, so one would know with certainty that one is in grace, which is plainly false.

alalal-e82539-d1e202.summary: Rejects restricting the claim to faith alone, since in De Trinitate VIII Augustine gives examples of faith, justice, charity and temperance, meaning everything in the soul by essence.

alalal-e82539-d1e222.summary: Rejects another reply, that one knows one's present state of grace but not one's perseverance: everyone would then know with certainty whether he is in grace, more surely than what he sees with his eyes, which each one's conscience shows to be false.

alalal-e82539-d1e251.summary: Adopts the view that, following Augustine, knowing that coincides with acquaintance ('nosse'), holding the knowledge of a thing within oneself, differs from knowing by discernment and thought ('cogitare'), which distinguishes a known thing from others.

alalal-e82539-d1e273.summary: Distinguishes two certitudes: the certitude of acquaintance, greater the more nobly the knowledge is possessed, by which nothing is so certain as what is in the soul by essence, though with degrees; and the certitude of discriminating knowledge, which considers a thing's proper differences in act and is greater the more its differences and properties have been investigated.
claims: Habitual acquaintance with what is in the soul is most certain, but discriminating knowledge of it may be lacking.

alalal-e82539-d1e308.summary: To the objection that the soul could turn to its own virtues and discern them at will, since understanding requires only assimilation: as Augustine asks why the soul, present to itself, seeks itself, the answer is that in this life the intellect is joined to phantasms and receives only from them; to discern what it has by essence it must get further knowledge from phantasms, learning to discern faith through its works and matter. So the soul can turn only to what it acquires by discovery or teaching, and to the rest imperfectly, through a confused habit of universal principles, as Boethius says in the Consolation.
claims: In this life the intellect depends on phantasms and cannot directly discern even what is in it by essence.
One discerns one's own faith through its works, not by direct intuition.

alalal-e82539-d1e383.summary: Continues with Boethius' verses: the mind, buried in blind members, cannot discern the fine connections of things; it has not wholly forgotten itself but holds the sum while losing the particulars, so the seeker neither fully knows nor is wholly ignorant, and by reconsidering what was seen on high adds the forgotten parts.

alalal-e82539-d1e430.summary: Explains that the 'sum seen on high' is the clouded knowledge in the confused, innate habit of the most universal principles; otherwise, as Augustine says, one would not recognise having found what one sought, nor seek or desire it, since one cannot seek or desire what is in no way known, as Aristotle also holds at the end of Posterior Analytics II.
claims: Inquiry presupposes an innate, confused knowledge of universal principles.

alalal-e82539.summary: Article 15 asks how Augustine can say that one holds one's faith with most certain knowledge, when Scripture denies that anyone knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred. Albert rejects two replies: that one sees faith without knowing whether it is sanctifying, and that one knows one's present state but not one's perseverance. Both would make people certain of being in grace, which conscience shows to be false. Following Augustine, he distinguishes the certitude of acquaintance ('nosse'), by which what is in the soul by essence is most certainly possessed, from the certitude of discriminating knowledge ('cogitare'). In this life the intellect depends on phantasms, so it can discern even its own virtues only through their works and through teaching, having of other things only a confused habit of universal principles. Boethius and Aristotle illustrate the point: inquiry presupposes such an innate habit.
claims: One possesses one's own faith with the certitude of acquaintance but cannot thereby discern with certainty that one is in grace.
In this life the intellect depends on phantasms and discerns even its own habits only through their works.
Inquiry presupposes an innate, confused knowledge of universal principles.
